newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin faces post-op risks, West could lend hand.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin faces post-op risks, West could lend hand.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin's failing heart is causing concern around the world. But his liver, lungs, kidneys or another vital organ may pose the biggest threat to his life, leading international cardiologists said on Tuesday.

Gathering in Moscow for an unrelated symposium, foreign and Russian experts said Western expertise and equipment could be needed to help the president through a minefield of possible complications after his planned heart bypass operation.
"The post-operative problems are the most serious risk," Bagrat Alekyan, a leading heart specialist at Moscow's Academy of Medical Sciences, told Reuters.
"Technically the operation can be done without problems. These days the problems do not lie with the heart bypass but rather with how to deal with the patient afterwards.
"I think the whole medical council...is considering this very problem -- how to pull the president through the post-operative period," Alekyan said.

A council of doctors, including U.S. bypass pioneer Michael DeBakey, is likely to meet on Wednesday to decide if and when to perform the bypass operation, which would graft in veins to relieve the 65-year-old Yeltsin's clogged arteries.
Renat Akchurin, the man expected to lead the team, has said it could be another two months before the president is well enough, if ever, to go under the knife.
"It is a very serious decision for these people," said Washington-based cardiac specialist Robert Wallace, adding that post-operative complications may pose the most difficult hurdle.

German surgeon Hans Borst said the chance gathering of foreign specialists in Moscow this week gave Russian doctors a vital opportunity to tap a pool of expertise in post-operative complications, possibly more developed than in Russia.

"That might be the most important part of this operation because apparently he has any number of risk factors outside his heart," said Borst, citing liver, lungs and kidneys as well as damage to the heart muscle itself from two or three previous heart attacks.
"It might become a very rough ride during the intensive care following the operation," he added. "I think a little help from the West would be quite opportune."

Experts in the treatment of "high-risk patients", as well as specialised drugs and equipment not readily available in Russia, could help if Yeltsin suffered from any of a number of potential problems after a successful bypass, Borst said.
"This is really our daily bread. The methodology of this part of surgery is very far advanced in all the Western countries. It might not be that far advanced in Russia."
Alekyan said the relatively smaller volume of cardiac surgery in Russia compared to the West meant "experience here is not comparable".
"Generally speaking, we have good surgery," he said. "But there are problems with post-operative treatment."

He cited as an example the fact that bypass patients, without complications, typically took a week or more before getting back on their feet -- almost twice as long as is normal in the best Western centres.
Alekyan noted that many Russian politicians and other personalities choose to go abroad for heart surgery but said the president had insisted he would be operated on "by our people".
"It's a matter of national prestige (for the Russians)," said Borst.
